mainTopic: End of the first משנה (23 judges, city size), then the גמרא on why the משנה lists גזילות וחבלות, and why admissions and loans need three judges but not מומחין.
overview: This amud finishes the first משנה of סנהדרין. A סנהדרין קטנה has 23 judges because a court may not have an even number. The משנה then gives the minimum population a city needs for its own סנהדרין: 120, or 230 according to רבי נחמיה. The גמרא asks why the משנה lists robbery and injury separately from money cases. רבי אבהו answers that the משנה uses a 'מה הן' style: 'money cases' is the heading, and robbery and injury define it, leaving out admissions and loans. A צריכא shows that both phrases are needed. The גמרא then explains that admissions and loans still need three judges, but not expert judges (מומחין). It asks whether this fits עירוב פרשיות. It answers that by Torah law experts would be needed, but רבי חנינא's teaching about דרישה וחקירה explains why they are not. That teaching continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A court cannot be even, so 22 becomes 23
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes its count of judges for a סנהדרין קטנה. Because a court may not have an even number of judges, one more is added, giving 23.
steps.simpleTranslation: A court may not have an even number of judges, so we add one more. That gives us twenty-three.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is finishing its count of how many judges sit on a small סנהדרין. Earlier in the משנה it reached 22. Now it adds one more judge so the number is not even.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An even court could split exactly down the middle and never reach a decision. So the משנה adds one judge to the 22 it already counted. That is where the famous number 23 comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: An evenly balanced court, meaning a court with an even number of judges
We add
Twenty-three, the size of a סנהדרין קטנה

steps.whatToRemember: A סנהדרין קטנה has 23 judges. The last judge is added only so the court is not even.

phrases.english: And a court may not be evenly numbered,
so they add one more to them.
So here there are twenty-three.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין בֵּית דִּין שָׁקוּל, מוֹסִיפִין עֲלֵיהֶם עוֹד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's count of judges, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A court may not be even. One judge is added to the 22, giving 23.

steps.title: How big a city must be to have a סנהדרין
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks how many people a city needs to deserve its own סנהדרין. The ת״ק says 120. רבי נחמיה says 230, based on the officers of tens.
steps.simpleTranslation: How many people must live in a city for it to be fit for a סנהדרין? One hundred and twenty. רבי נחמיה says two hundred and thirty, matching the officers who were each in charge of ten people.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the minimum population a city needs before it can set up its own סנהדרין. There are two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic within the same משנה. The first part was about how many judges sit. This part is about which cities may have a court of 23 at all. רבי נחמיה ties the number to the system of שרי עשרות, where one officer was set over every ten people.

keyTerms.meaning: Fit or eligible to have a סנהדרין
One hundred and twenty
Officers of tens, leaders each in charge of ten people

phrases.english: And how many must be in the city
for it to be fit for a Sanhedrin?
One hundred and twenty.
Rabbi Nechemya says: two hundred and thirty,
corresponding to the officers of tens.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה יְהֵא בָּעִיר וּתְהֵא רְאוּיָה לְסַנְהֶדְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the number of judges to the size a city needs to have such a court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city needs 120 people for a סנהדרין. רבי נחמיה says 230.

steps.title: Aren't robbery and injury already money cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by challenging the wording of the משנה. Why does it list גזילות וחבלות separately, when they are clearly דיני ממונות?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Are robbery and injury not money cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It challenges the wording at the start of the פרק, where the משנה lists 'money cases' and then 'robbery and injury' as if they were two separate things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Robbery and injury are obviously money cases, since the court decides how much someone must pay. So listing them separately looks repetitive. The question is about the משנה's wording, not about the law of three judges itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? An opening for a surprised challenge
Robbery cases
Personal injury cases
Money cases

phrases.english: Gemara
Is that to say that robbery and injury
phrases.notes: This goes back to the opening line of the פרק, which lists money cases and then robbery and injury.

phrases.english: are not money cases?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ גְּזֵילוֹת וְחַבָּלוֹת לָאו דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first move of the גמרא. It goes back to the opening words of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's listing of גזילות וחבלות as separate from דיני ממונות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Robbery and injury fall inside money cases, so listing them separately seems repetitive.

steps.title: רבי אבהו: read it as 'What are these money cases?'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו explains that the משנה is not listing two separate things. 'Money cases' is a heading, and 'robbery and injury' explains which money cases are meant. Admissions and loans are excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: The משנה is teaching in a 'what are they' style. What are these money cases? Robbery and injury. But admissions and loans are not included.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers the challenge by rereading the משנה. The second phrase explains the first phrase instead of adding to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'money cases' works like a heading, and 'robbery and injury' defines it. That narrows the rule in the משנה to robbery and injury. Admissions and loans are left out of this line.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches in a 'what are they' style: a heading followed by an explanation
Admissions, cases where a person admits he owes money
Loan cases

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אבהו is saying admissions and loans need no court at all. He is only saying they are not what this line of the משנה is talking about.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu said:
It teaches in a 'what are they' style,
phrases.notes: He means the משנה should be read with an unspoken question: 'What are they?'

phrases.english: What are these money cases?
Robbery and injury.
But admissions and loans: no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: מָה הֵן קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3 by rereading the משנה's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the text: the second phrase defines the first instead of adding to it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה lists two separate categories, which would be repetitive.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Money cases' is a heading, explained as robbery and injury only. Admissions and loans are excluded.
steps.whyThisMatters: This reading narrows the משנה's three-judge line to robbery and injury, which shapes how the rest of the sugya reads the משנה.

steps.title: Why the words 'robbery and injury' are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that both phrases are necessary. If the משנה had said only 'money cases', we would include admissions and loans. So it added 'robbery and injury' to narrow it down.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both phrases are needed. If the משנה had said only 'money cases', I would have thought it includes even admissions and loans. So it taught 'robbery and injury'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a צריכא, which explains why each of the two phrases in the משנה is needed. This step explains the need for 'robbery and injury'. The next step explains the need for 'money cases'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Money cases' alone is a wide term that would cover admissions and loans too. Adding 'robbery and injury' narrows it to those cases only.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary: both parts are needed
For if it had taught
I would have thought, the mistaken first assumption

phrases.english: And it is necessary,
for if it had taught only 'money cases',
I would have said even admissions and loans are included.
So it taught 'robbery and injury'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבי אבהו's reading by showing that the phrase 'robbery and injury' is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא: shows that each phrase is needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only 'money cases', admissions and loans would be included.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Robbery and injury' limits the heading to those cases.

steps.title: Why the words 'money cases' are also needed
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה had said only 'robbery and injury', we would think these were just examples, chosen because the source for three judges is written about such cases. Then admissions and loans would be included too. The heading 'money cases' with the 'מה הן' style shows the list is meant to limit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught 'robbery and injury' without teaching 'money cases', I would have said the same law applies even to admissions and loans. I would have said it mentions robbery and injury only because the main place where 'three' is written in the Torah is about robbery and injury.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second half of the צריכא, showing why the heading 'money cases' is also needed. The next steps explain the source behind this mistaken assumption and then conclude the צריכא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the heading, 'robbery and injury' could look like mere examples, picked only because the Torah's source for three judges speaks about such cases. The heading together with the 'מה הן' style tells us the list is exact and leaves out admissions and loans.

keyTerms.meaning: The same law applies
The main or primary source
That are written in the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אבהו, both phrases together mean that the משנה's line covers only robbery and injury. Each phrase is needed: one keeps admissions and loans out, and the other shows the list is exact, not just examples.

phrases.english: And if it had taught 'robbery and injury',
and had not taught 'money cases',
I would have said the same law applies
even to admissions and loans.
And the fact that it teaches 'robbery and injury'
would be because the main place where the 'three' are written,
phrases.notes: He means the פסוקים in the Torah that the rule of three judges is learned from.

phrases.english: they are written about robbery and injury.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי תְּנָא גְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲבָלוֹת, וְלָא קָתָנֵי דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the צריכא begun in step 5 by explaining the need for the other phrase.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both phrases are necessary. Together they show that this line of the משנה covers only robbery and injury, not admissions and loans.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only 'robbery and injury', these would look like examples, and admissions and loans would be included too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The heading 'money cases' is needed so that 'robbery and injury' reads as an exact list.

steps.title: Robbery comes from the verse, and injury is treated like robbery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that robbery is written directly in the פסוק about judges. Injury is treated the same way, because hurting a body is no different from hurting property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Robbery: as it is written, 'The owner of the house shall come near to the judges.' Injury: what difference is there between hurting someone's body and hurting his property!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the reasoning from step 6. It shows exactly how robbery and injury connect to the פסוק that teaches three judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the owner of the house coming before the judges is about a watchman suspected of taking the item, so it is a robbery case. Injury is not written there directly. The גמרא brings it in with simple logic: harming a person's body is just like harming his belongings.

keyTerms.meaning: Robbery cases
Injury cases (one person hurts another)
The owner of the house (here, the watchman holding the item)
Here it means 'the judges', not God
What difference does it make to me (both cases are the same)

phrases.english: Robbery, as it is written:
"The owner of the house shall come near to the judges."
phrases.notes: שמות 22:7. Here אֱלֹהִים means the judges.

phrases.english: Injuries –
what difference is it to me if he hurt his body,
or if he hurt his property!
phrases.notes: Meaning: the פסוק talks about property, and hurting a body is treated the same way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the step 6 idea that robbery and injury might only be examples taken from the פסוק itself.
steps.raayaObject: That robbery and injury are the cases tied directly to the פסוק requiring judges
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 22:7, plus the logic that harming a body is like harming property

steps.title: So the תנא taught both: 'What are money cases? Robbery and injury'
steps.stepSummary: The צריכא concludes: since each phrase alone could mislead, the תנא of the משנה used both in a 'what are they' style. Money cases are only robbery and injury, not admissions and loans.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore the תנא taught: What are money cases? Robbery and injury. But admissions and loans are not included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the צריכא. Since neither phrase alone would work, the תנא wrote both together in a 'what are they' style, exactly as רבי אבהו read it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Money cases' alone would include admissions and loans. 'Robbery and injury' alone could look like examples taken from the פסוק. Putting both together as a heading plus a definition makes the list exact, which is רבי אבהו's reading from step 4. It also sets up the next question: left out of which rule?

keyTerms.meaning: Here: so the תנא taught (closing the צריכא)

steps.whatToRemember: The phrase 'money cases' in the משנה means only robbery and injury. Admissions and loans are left out.

phrases.english: So the tanna taught: What are money cases?
Robbery and injury.
But admissions and loans – no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the צריכא of steps 5-7: because each phrase alone could mislead, the תנא used both.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'מה הן' list limits money cases to robbery and injury. Admissions and loans are excluded.

steps.title: Excluded from which rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which rule admissions and loans are left out of.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question that opens the next discussion: what practical rule doesn't apply to admissions and loans?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying admissions and loans are 'not included' is incomplete until we know which rule they are left out of. The next steps try out possible answers.

keyTerms.meaning: And for what? (which rule is meant?)

phrases.english: And regarding what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what practical difference the exclusion in step 8 makes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which rule applies to robbery and injury but not to admissions and loans

steps.title: It can't mean they need fewer than three judges
steps.stepSummary: One idea is that admissions and loans don't need three judges. רבי אבהו rejects that, because two judges are never valid for money cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say they don't need three judges, didn't רבי אבהו say: if two judges judged money cases, everyone agrees their ruling is not valid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests an answer, that admissions and loans don't need three judges, and right away knocks it down with a statement of רבי אבהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו says every money case, loans included, needs at least three judges. Since everyone agrees on this, the difference between the two groups can't be the number of judges.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
We need
According to everyone
Their ruling is not a valid ruling

phrases.english: If you say that we don't need three,
but didn't Rabbi Abahu say:
two who judged money cases,
according to everyone, their ruling is not a ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא דְּלָא בָּעֵינַן שְׁלֹשָׁה, וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests a first answer to step 9's question and rejects it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that admissions and loans can be judged by fewer than three judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אבהו says everyone agrees that two judges are invalid for any money case, so loans also need three.

steps.title: The difference is about expert judges
steps.stepSummary: The real difference is that admissions and loans do not need expert judges (מומחין).
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: that we don't need experts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its answer: admissions and loans still need three judges, but they don't have to be expert, ordained judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All money cases need three judges. Only robbery and injury need מומחין. So the משנה's list tells us which cases need expert judges.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (brings a new answer after the first is rejected)
Expert, ordained judges

steps.confusionAlert: Admissions and loans still need three judges. The only difference is that the judges don't have to be experts.

phrases.english: Rather: that we don't need experts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer from step 10 with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines which rule the exclusion refers to
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Admissions and loans might not need three judges
steps.terutzMaskana: Admissions and loans need three judges, but not experts
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the well-known split: robbery and injury need expert judges, while everyday loan cases can be judged by any three people.

steps.title: The dilemma: are the Torah sections read together or not?
steps.stepSummary: Either way the תנא holds, there is a problem. If the sections are joined, loans should need experts too. If they are not joined, there is no source that loans need three judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does he hold? If he holds the sections are mixed together here, he should also require experts. And if he holds they are not mixed together here, why do I need three?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 11 with a two-sided question about how the תנא reads the verses in שמות 22.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If עירוב פרשיות applies, the verses about loans and robbery count as one unit, so the expert rule should cover loans too. If it does not apply, the source for three judges is written only about robbery, so loans would have no source for three. The answer from step 11, three judges but no experts, doesn't fit either reading.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds (his position)
Mixing of sections: different topics in the verses are read as one unit
He should also require
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: What does he hold?

phrases.aramaic: אִי קָסָבַר עֵירוּב פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת כָּתוּב כָּאן,
phrases.english: If he holds that a mixing of sections is written here,
phrases.notes: The different cases in these פסוקים are read together, so a rule said about one applies to all.

phrases.english: he should also require experts.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי קָסָבַר אֵין עֵירוּב פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת כָּתוּב כָּאן,
phrases.english: And if he holds that no mixing of sections is written here,
why do I need three?
phrases.notes: He means three judges for admissions and loans, since the source for three is written about robbery.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָסָבַר? אִי קָסָבַר עֵירוּב פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת כָּתוּב כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer from step 11 by asking what source reading it rests on.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that admissions and loans need three judges but not experts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma. Joined sections would require experts for loans too. Separate sections would give no source for three judges in loans. Neither reading gives 'three but not experts'.

steps.title: The sections are joined, but experts are not needed because of רבי חנינא
steps.stepSummary: The תנא holds the sections are joined (עירוב פרשיות), so by right loans should need expert judges. They do not, because of a reason given by רבי חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the תנא holds that the Torah sections are mixed together here. So by strict law, loans should need expert judges too. The reason we do not require experts is because of רבי חנינא's teaching.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 12 by choosing one side: the sections really are joined. It admits that experts should be needed, and says a separate reason, from רבי חנינא, removes that need.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said that if the sections are joined, loans should need experts. The גמרא accepts that this is true by basic Torah law. The difference between loans and other money cases now comes from רבי חנינא's teaching, not from the verses.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (keeping the original view and explaining it)
A mixing of Torah sections, where rules from one section apply to the other
By right, by strict law
Expert judges with סמיכה

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying loans are outside the category of cases that need experts by Torah law. It agrees they should need experts. A separate reason explains why we do not require them in practice.

phrases.english: Actually, he holds:
phrases.notes: "He" is the תנא of our משנה, read the way רבי אבהו explained it.

phrases.english: a mixing of the sections is written here,
and by right he should require experts too.
And the fact that we do not require experts
is because of Rabbi Chanina's teaching,

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם קָסָבַר עֵירוּב פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת כָּתוּב כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided challenge of Step 12 by accepting that the sections are joined.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts one side of the challenge and explains the remaining difference with an outside reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the sections are joined, loans must need expert judges, which goes against Step 11.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sections are joined and by Torah law experts would be needed. The lack of an expert requirement comes from רבי חנינא's teaching.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: money cases also need careful questioning of witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא teaches that by Torah law both money cases and capital cases require inquiry and interrogation of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי חנינא said: By Torah law, both money cases and capital cases need careful questioning of the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי חנינא's teaching, which is the source mentioned in Step 13. This sets up the explanation of why experts are not needed. The quote continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דרישה וחקירה means checking the witnesses' details closely, like time and place, to catch any contradiction. רבי חנינא says the Torah requires this even in money cases, not only in capital cases. The rest of his statement will show how this connects to not requiring experts.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law (as opposed to a rabbinic rule)
Money cases
Capital cases (life and death)
Inquiry and interrogation: detailed questioning of witnesses

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the key to the whole answer. It shows that the Torah's basic rules for money cases are strict, and the next lines will explain why the חכמים did not require all of them.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Chanina said:
By Torah law,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת וְאֶחָד דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת
phrases.english: both money cases and capital cases
need inquiry and interrogation of witnesses,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the teaching of רבי חנינא that Step 13 relied on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, money cases and capital cases both require דרישה וחקירה of the witnesses.
